slides.headline:
Korean cooking,
minus the garlic.
slides.subline: Balwoo Gongyang, Jongno — Buddhist temple cuisine, run by the order itself since 2009

slides.label: aromatics a temple kitchen will not use — garlic, green onion, chives, wild chives and asafoetida
slides.note: Together they are called the ohsinchae. Buddhist practice holds that their pungency stirs the mind and gets in the way of meditation, so temple cooking leaves all five out. Source: Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism (koreatemplefood.com)

items.t: Meat, fish, and any stock made from them
items.d: Temple food uses no animal products; the order's own guidance names dairy as the single exception
Garlic and green onion sit under most Korean home cooking. Here they are simply absent
Depth is built from mushroom powder, kelp powder, soy sauce and doenjang instead
The official Seoul city listing notes none is sold on the premises

slides.title:
Cooking by
subtraction.
slides.body:
Take away meat, take away stock, take away garlic and onion, and most cuisines have nothing left to stand on. Temple cooking has spent roughly 1,700 years working out what does.

What carries the flavour is time rather than pungency: soy sauce and soybean paste aged in temple jars, dried mushrooms, kelp, seasonal mountain greens picked and preserved when they are ready. The constraint is the technique.

And this is not a chef's personal project. Balwoo Gongyang is operated directly by the Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism, the Jogye Order's cultural body, which opened it in 2009 to keep that tradition legible to people who will never live in a temple.

caption:
Most Korean cooking starts with garlic. This kitchen removes it.

Balwoo Gongyang in Jongno serves Buddhist temple cuisine — no meat, no garlic, no onion — and is run directly by the Jogye Order's cultural body. Courses from 36,000 won, reservation only.

Prices and hours change, so confirm before you go.
